historical_territory: Sự tương phản giữa một Sumerian literary tradition về sau, nơi writing mang một thông điệp vượt quá khả năng lặp lại của messenger, và trạng thái sớm hơn của proto-cuneiform, nơi các dấu được chứng thực chủ yếu trong công việc hành chính và chưa cho thấy continuous speech hay underlying language một cách chắc chắn.

historical_change.from: Early proto-cuneiform primarily stabilizes quantities, categories and administrative relations while continuous speech and underlying language remain only weakly recoverable.
historical_change.to: Later cuneiform can carry extended language, and Sumerian literary tradition can imagine a written message as something that travels beyond the oral memory of its messenger.

world.tradition: Sumerian literary composition Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta
world.represented_problem: a substantial and extensive royal message exceeds the messenger's ability to repeat it orally
world.represented_response: Enmerkar places the message on clay as a tablet and sends it to Aratta
world.represented_use: written message travels while the messenger no longer needs to reproduce the whole message from memory

primitives.time_scope: literary tradition surviving in Old Babylonian witnesses; narrated setting is earlier and not used here as a dated historical event
primitives.place_scope: Sumerian literary tradition concerning Uruk/Kulaba and Aratta

world.composition: Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta (CDLI composite Q000369)

primitives.place_scope: surviving manuscript tradition including Nippur and other Mesopotamian witnesses

world.period: Uruk IV and early proto-cuneiform horizon
world.dominant_attested_use: administrative recording of quantities, categories and related institutional information
world.language_visibility: continuous speech and the underlying language are not securely recoverable across the early material
world.phonetic_capacity: rare possible phonetic/rebus uses exist early, while consistent phonetic writing is clearer later

primitives.time_scope: Uruk IV–III, late fourth to early third millennium BCE
primitives.place_scope: Uruk cultural sphere, especially southern Mesopotamia

world.left: later Sumerian literary imagination of a written message carrying words beyond a messenger's oral capacity
world.relation: can be set in qualified contrast with
world.right: earliest substantial proto-cuneiform material dominated by administrative relations with limited recoverable speech/language
world.temporal_scope: comparison between late-fourth-millennium early writing and much later surviving literary witnesses
world.qualification: the contrast motivates a question about changing writing capacities; it does not prove that the poem preserves a historical memory of that change

primitives.time_scope: analytical contrast across early writing and later literary tradition

world.left: growth in administrative and institutional scale
world.relation: co-occurred with and created pressure compatible with
world.right: greater demand for records and authentication
world.qualification: co-occurrence does not establish a sole cause or one-way causal sequence

primitives.place_scope: Urban and institutional contexts in southern Mesopotamia represented in the approved sources

boundaries.rule: Documented means the literary tradition is attested; it does not mean Enmerkar historically invented writing or that the narrated exchange occurred as described.
Frame the scene as later literary memory/etiology when listener could otherwise hear it as an eyewitness origin account.
Manuscript date does not equal the date when every element of the tradition was first composed or orally circulated; it does bound what survives directly.
Predominantly administrative preserved material does not prove administration was the only use or cause; survival and excavation are selective.
Undetermined underlying language does not mean the writers lacked spoken language or that no early sign ever had phonetic value.
Do not label the entire earliest corpus securely Sumerian.
Do not narrate the literary scene as a surviving oral memory of the actual invention unless separate evidence is supplied.
Do not turn the contrast into a deterministic administration-to-speech ladder; functions overlap and intermediate evidence is incomplete.
Administration is a major formation pressure, not a monocausal explanation.
Do not turn administrative pressure or institutional co-occurrence into a sole-cause or one-way causal verdict.
Keep documented tradition, historical event and scholarly hypothesis distinct: an attested literary scene may carry narrative weight without being promoted to eyewitness history or causal proof.

writer_contract: Historical Substrate is a source-anchored set of historical conditions, documented traditions, qualified interpretations and bounded reconstructions. Epistemic status controls how each may be narrated: a documented tradition proves the tradition is attested, not that its narrated event occurred. The Writer may connect supported material into an explicitly qualified possibility, but compatibility must not be turned into proof.
